[...] El acento puede recaer en cualquiera de las tres últimas sílabas, aunque las posiciones últimas y penúltimas forman la gran mayoría de la localización del acento. El acento es distintivo a nivel semántico, como entre /ˈkasa/ ‘casa’ y /kaˈsa/ ‘casar’ o /ˈduda/ ‘duda’ y /duˈda/ ‘dudar’. new_statements.translation: Stress may fall on any of the last three syllables, although the final and penultimate positions account for the great majority of stress placements. Stress is semantically distinctive, as between /ˈkasa/ 'house' and /kaˈsa/ 'to marry' or /ˈduda/ 'doubt' and /duˈda/ 'to doubt'. [...] In the basic-vocabulary sample, excluding monosyllables, stress falls on the penultimate syllable in 61.6% of words, on the final syllable in 37.7%, and on the antepenult in 0.6%. [...] Taking into account the relation between lexical categories and stress, verbs typically stress the final syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically fixed and contrastive, confined to the last three syllables (three-syllable window as in Spanish); penult is the statistical default (61.6%), final stress is common (37.7%, and the norm for verbs), antepenult is rare (0.6%). In most words stress reproduces the primary stress of the Spanish or Tagalog etymon, so it is not predictable from phonological shape.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned only for compounds and reduplications (p. 62): primary stress normally on the second element; occasionally primary on the first and secondary on the second, e.g. /buskabida/ 'work' [ˌbuskaˈbida] / [ˈbuskaˌbida]; reduplications may stress the second element or each element separately in slow careful speech.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs tyéni 'have', kyéri 'want', pwédi 'can', sábi 'know' (from Spanish 3sg forms) are penult-stressed against the final-stress verb norm; unstressed-vowel reduction can delete syllables (/aˈgora/ > [ˈgora]); free variation in some words (/manong/ [ˈma.nong]/[maˈnong], /ternate/, /kelya/, /bali-kohri/), attributed to intonation and final lengthening, unexplained; function words (TMA markers, negator, pronouns, plural/object markers, prepositions, adverbial clitics) are unstressed clitics attached to stressed words (§2.6.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (palabra fonológica, one main stress per word); based on natural-speech samples checked against isolated fragments, analysed in Praat 5.1.17; percentages from a basic-vocabulary sample (annex 2). The APiCS survey chapter (Sippola 2013, saved) gives the one-line version: stress contrastive, verbs generally final.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Ternate Chabacano (Ternateño, 'CT' in Sippola 2011) as spoken in Ternate, Cavite, Philippines — this is tern1248 itself, not a sub-dialect. Note the our source list record lists countries 'ID', but the language is Philippine (latlon 14.28/120.72 is Cavite); the sister variety Cavite Chabacano is chav1241 and was not used for the statement.
